identification.bodyShape: Smallest hammerhead species; streamlined body typical of coastal Sphyrnidae, with the genus's laterally expanded head (cephalofoil).
identificationTraits: Head is broad, smooth, and shovel- or spade-shaped rather than the strongly T-shaped, laterally scalloped head of scalloped hammerhead or the broad, flat, near-straight-edged head of great hammerhead — the single clearest mark separating bonnethead from the two federally/state-prohibited hammerheads it could otherwise be mistaken for.

Sexually dimorphic head shape unique among sharks: adult females have an evenly rounded head margin, while adult males develop a distinct forward bulge in the center of the head once they reach maturity (NOAA).
Scattered small dark markings on the dorsal surface and flanks over an otherwise gray, tan, or greenish back and paler belly.
identification.coloration: Gray, tan, or greenish above with scattered small dark markings, paler below.
identification.sexualDimorphism: Unique among sharks: mature males show a distinct central bulge on the head; mature females have an evenly rounded head margin (NOAA).
identification.adultAppearance: A small, gray-to-greenish shark with a smooth, spade-shaped head, distinguishable from both larger hammerhead species by head shape alone.

similarSpecies.name: Great hammerhead (Sphyrna mokarran)
similarSpecies.distinction: Federally and Florida-state PROHIBITED. Has a much broader, flatter, nearly straight-edged head and grows far larger; NOAA's own comparison note describes bonnethead's shovel-shaped head and roughly 5 ft maximum size specifically to distinguish it from great hammerhead.

similarSpecies.name: Scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini)
similarSpecies.distinction: Federally and Florida-state PROHIBITED. Has a distinctly scalloped (wavy-edged) hammer with a central notch, unlike bonnethead's smooth spade-shaped head.

similarSpecies.name: Smooth hammerhead (Sphyrna zygaena)
similarSpecies.distinction: Florida-state PROHIBITED (per FWC's prohibited list). Has a smooth-edged but much broader, more rectangular head and grows considerably larger than bonnethead.

identification.commonAnglingSize: Most inshore recreational catches fall in the 2-4 ft range typical of the species; no minimum size currently applies in either federal or Florida state waters (see targetContext).
identification.typicalWeight: Not resolved to a typical figure; NOAA gives a maximum documented weight only (see maximumDocumentedSize).
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: NOAA: maximum length about 5 ft, maximum documented weight 24 lb.
identification.longevity: NOAA: estimated maximum age 18 years (females), 16 years (males).

social.note: Widely described in the sources reviewed as common in bays, estuaries, and grass flats, consistent with loose group association typical of small coastal Sphyrnidae; a formal schooling-structure study was not reviewed this session.

feedingStrategy.note: NOAA and the peer-reviewed literature describe an omnivorous diet: benthic invertebrate prey (crabs, shrimp, snails) taken by grubbing/benthic feeding, alongside fish and — unusually for a shark — genuine digestion and assimilation of seagrass, not just incidental ingestion.

behavior.spawningBehavior: Roughly 5-month gestation; 4-14 live pups born in late summer or early fall, about 12 in at birth. Recorded as conservation context only; no pupping location is identified.

diet.primaryNote: NOAA describes an omnivorous diet of fish, crabs, snails, and shrimp 'in addition to grazing on seagrass — making them unique among sharks for this herbivorous behavior.' This is corroborated by peer-reviewed work (Leigh, Papastamatiou and German 2018, Proceedings of the Royal Society B) showing bonnethead sharks genuinely digest and assimilate seagrass rather than merely ingesting it incidentally while hunting benthic prey among grass blades — a rare, real, sourceable case of partial herbivory/omnivory in an elasmobranch. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event, and seagrass consumption specifically should not be read as a targetable forage behavior — it is digestive/nutritional biology, not a bait cue.

lifeStageDiet.adult: Crustaceans (crabs, shrimp), mollusks (snails), small fish, and digested seagrass, per NOAA and the peer-reviewed seagrass-digestion study.

diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity described here is not proof that a bait event is occurring on any given day. Observed current forage still comes from a user observation or Hatch Match. Seagrass digestion capacity in particular is a biological/nutritional finding, not a presentation cue.

seasonal_calendar.overview: A small, shallow-water hammerhead common on grass flats and in bays and estuaries year-round across its warm-temperate to tropical range, with late-summer/early-fall pupping. Month-by-month habitat shifts were not resolved from a sourced account this session.

entries.habitatClass: Shallow grass flats, sand holes, and bay/estuary edges.
